title: Countable and uncountable 2
subtitle: a paper / some paper
summary: Learn which nouns change meaning when they are countable or uncountable, and which common nouns (advice, luggage, news ...) are always uncountable.

lesson.heading: The same word, two meanings
lesson.text: Many nouns are sometimes countable and sometimes uncountable. Usually there is a difference in meaning: the countable form is one specific thing, the uncountable form is the material or the idea in general.

examples.text: Did you hear **a noise** just now?
I can't work here. There's too much **noise**.

lesson.heading: Compare
rows: I bought **a paper** to read. (= a newspaper)
I need some **paper** to write on. (= material)
There's **a hair** in my soup! (= one single hair)
This is **a nice room**. (= a room in a house)
You can't sit here. There isn't **room**. (= space)
I had some interesting **experiences** while I was travelling.
I was offered the job because I had a lot of **experience**. (not experiences)
Enjoy your trip. Have **a great time**!
I can't wait. I don't have **time**.

lesson.heading: Drinks
lesson.text: Coffee, tea, juice, beer and other drinks are normally uncountable. But you can say **a coffee** (= a cup of coffee), **two coffees** (= two cups) and so on.

lesson.heading: Nouns that are usually uncountable
lesson.text: These nouns are normally uncountable: **accommodation, advice, baggage, behaviour, bread, chaos, damage, furniture, information, luck, luggage, news, permission, progress, scenery, traffic, weather, work**. We do not use a/an with them, and they are not usually plural.

examples.text: I'm going to buy some **bread**. *or* ... **a loaf of bread**.
Enjoy your holiday! I hope you have good **weather**.
Where are you going to put all your **furniture**?
Let me know if you need more **information**.

lesson.heading: travel, trip and journey
lesson.text: **Travel** (noun) means travelling in general and is uncountable. We do not say 'a travel' to mean a single trip - use **a trip** or **a journey**.

examples.text: They spend a lot of money on **travel**.

lesson.text: Uncountable nouns take a singular verb: *The news **is** good*, *This furniture **is** mine*, *There **was** a lot of traffic*.

exercises.prompt: The engine is making ___. What is it?
exercises.explanation: One specific noise, so noise is countable here: a strange noise.

exercises.prompt: We live near a busy road, so ___.
options: there are a lot of noises
there's a lot of a noise
exercises.explanation: Noise in general is uncountable: a lot of noise.

exercises.statement: We really enjoyed our holiday. We had great time.
exercises.explanation: We had a great time. When time means an occasion or experience it is countable, so it needs a.

exercises.prompt: Be careful. The window has been broken and there's ___ on the floor.
exercises.explanation: Here glass is the material, so it is uncountable: broken glass.

exercises.prompt: Did you have ___ when you were away?
exercises.explanation: Weather is uncountable: no a/an and no plural.

exercises.statement: Bad news don't make people happy.
exercises.explanation: Bad news doesn't make people happy. News is uncountable, not plural, so it takes a singular verb.

exercises.prompt: Our ___ from Paris to Moscow by train was very tiring.
exercises.explanation: Travel means travelling in general; for one particular trip we say a journey or a trip.

exercises.prompt: We have no ___, not even a bed or a table.
Carla's English is better than it was. She's made good ___.
exercises.explanation: Progress is uncountable, so no a/an and no plural.

exercises.prompt: Kate has done many interesting things. She could write a book about her ___.
exercises.explanation: Things that happened to her are countable experiences (uncountable experience = knowledge of a job).

exercises.prompt: What do you say in each situation? Match them.

pairs.left: Your friends have arrived at the station and you can't see any cases or bags.
You are at a tourist office and want to know about places to visit.
You want your teacher to help you choose your courses.
pairs.right: Can you give me some advice?

pairs.left: You call Tom to tell him you have got the job.
You are at the top of a mountain and can see a very long way.
pairs.right: It's a beautiful view, isn't it?

pairs.left: You look out of the window: it's cold, wet and windy.

exercises.prompt: Which of these nouns can take a/an and a plural, and which are normally uncountable?
